chapter_theme: Guided by the deity in the guise of a hunchbacked maid, Vijayai walks barefoot through the forest to a hermitage, where, after the narrator names a former-birth deed as the cause of her suffering, the women ascetics strip her of her ornaments one by one and she takes the ochre cloth and the widow's diet, keeping only a vow for her son; the deity entrusts her to them and leaves on a pretext, and the story turns to the city, where the merchant and his wife name the child Civakan and he grows on his foster mother's milk.

cast.role: Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother, now a fugitive widow
the deity who, in the form of the hunchback maid Chanbakamalai (314), guides Vijayai to the hermitage
the women ascetics of the hermitage who receive Vijayai
the merchant who took up and raises the newborn Civakan
Kantukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother; unnamed in these verses
the worthy elders who gather to name the child
the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by Kantukkatan
the dead king, Vijayai's husband, named in 350 and 352 as வேந்தன்

340.reading: Vijayai sets out, her anklets crying as if singing praise, her gold bells and girdle swaying and her spear-like eyes troubled, her whole coral-branch body wrapped in a cloak as thin as a spider's web.
340.event: Vijayai, wrapped in a thin cloak, sets out from the burning ground by night.
340.nuance: The ornaments she still wears here are the ones she will take off one by one in 349 to 353; the departure is dressed as a queen's procession, with the anklets as her only heralds.

341.reading: Her feet, so soft they shrink even from anicham pressed on cotton and from the nerunji's ripe fruit, curl and falter on the file-rough forest floor and bleed, while she breathes hot and walks on like a peacock swinging its arms, her waist bending.
341.event: Vijayai walks barefoot through the rough forest, her feet bleeding.
341.nuance: The conventional hyperbole of the tender foot that fears even the anicham flower is turned into a measure of real injury: the same feet now pour blood (குருதி கான்று).

342.reading: The queen, like the goddess who dwells in the lotus's pollen, and the hunchback with eyes like cupped palms crossed sharp-pebbled wastes and hills and reached a river with abundant water, so it is told.
342.event: Vijayai and the hunchbacked companion cross wastes and hills and reach a river.
342.nuance: The கூனி is the deity that took the form of the hunchback maid Chanbakamalai in 314; the verse keeps the disguise, so only the reader knows that the queen's companion is a god. என்பவே presents the journey as a report.

343.reading: When the thousand-rayed sun rose from the sea at the edge of the sky, the lingering darkness went away like the suffering of cruel deeds when old good deeds come to the front.

claims.claim: when good deeds of the past come to fruit, the suffering due to evil deeds departs

343.nuance: The doctrine is the vehicle of a simile for the dawn, not stated for its own sake, but the narrator places it at the moment the queen's night of loss ends, which presents her rescue as merit coming to fruit.

344.reading: Like a slender lightning-creeper fallen from a cloud and lying in a fragrant grove, the woman of long spear-like eyes lay resting on a fine cloth.
344.event: Vijayai lies down to rest by the river at dawn.
344.nuance: அணங்கு நுண் துகில் may mean a cloth fine enough for a goddess, or a cloth the deity spread; the verse does not say who laid it.

345.reading: Saying 'Night is over, my mother, long may you live, it is time', the companion strokes her feet with her hand; Vijayai opens her eyes, cries out in dismay and rises, like the bright moon rising from the crowded earth.
345.event: The hunchbacked companion wakes Vijayai at dawn and she rises.
345.nuance: The deity calls the queen எம் அனை, 'our mother', the word a servant uses; Vijayai's waking cry ஐயவோ shows that sleep has given her no forgetting.

346.reading: Swans with soft-feathered wings, peacocks and herds of deer in the soft fields, seeing again and again her musk-scented lovely body, gasp and, unable to bear it, weep.
346.event: The birds and deer of the forest weep at the sight of her.
346.nuance: The forest's creatures mourn as the palace women did in 292 to 296; the queen has no human mourners left.

347.reading: The creeper-like woman, because a deed of a former birth stood waiting for her, suffered this distress in this life, and she reached the hermitage where the great ascetics of right conduct perform their austerities.

claims.claim: a deed done in a former birth brings suffering in this life

347.nuance: The narrator names ஊழ்வினை of the former birth (உம்மை) as the cause of her suffering in this birth (இம்மை), after the earlier verses had blamed the minister's treachery and the king's infatuation; both causes stand in the story. The same verse carries her to the tapas grove, so the fruit of the old deed and the way out of it arrive together.

348.reading: The women ascetics all gather and receive her as if to embrace her shoulders, take her in, ease the pain of her feet, and, meaning to set her on the path of austerity, on a day when the moon stands in an auspicious asterism, begin to take off her fine ornaments.
348.event: The women ascetics receive Vijayai and begin to remove her ornaments to set her on the ascetic path.
348.nuance: The initiation waits for an auspicious day (நாள் உறத் திங்கள் ஊர): the turn to austerity is timed by the same astrology as a wedding, and it is the ascetic women, not Vijayai, who begin to strip the jewels.

349.reading: She takes off the precious gold garland and her necklace, while her musk-dressed hair, which had lain steeped in the smoke of black agil sweetened with honey on a takaram fire, grieves, and the bees and honey-bees grieve in song.
349.event: Vijayai removes her garland and necklace.
349.nuance: Each object she gives up is made to lament (புலம்ப three times), so the renunciation is felt by the things renounced; the verse does not yet say she cuts her hair.

350.reading: With her finger she removes the tilaka that shone like the moon on a fingernail, the gold makara earrings, the ornaments of her neck, and the pearls and gold on her breasts, which were nectar to the fierce-eyed king.
350.event: Vijayai removes her tilaka, earrings and breast ornaments.
350.nuance: Line 3 ties the breasts' adornment to the king's pleasure (வெம் கண் வேந்தற்கு அமிர்து ஆகி): what is put off is the queen's beauty as the dead husband's delight.

351.reading: Saying to the paired pearls that the makara clasp spilled on her soft bamboo-like shoulders, 'I worship you', she gives them up; she breaks the bangles on her arms and removes the gold rings from her fingers, so red they frighten the kanthal flower.
351.event: Vijayai takes leave of her armlet pearls, breaks her bangles and removes her rings.
351.nuance: தொழுதேன் உம்மை is a courteous farewell spoken to the jewels. Breaking the bangles (வளை கை உடைத்து) is the widow's sign, not only an ascetic's giving up of ornament.

352.reading: She gives up all the ornaments that shine on her hips, the flowered gold sash, the gold-fringed girdle and the jewelled band, telling them: 'The king has gone and looks on the heavenly women; he will not look at you; stop grieving.'
352.event: Vijayai takes off her girdle ornaments, telling them the king will not look at them again.

claims.claim: the king fallen in battle has gone to heaven, where celestial women are his company

352.nuance: She consoles the jewels as a widow might console her women: their purpose was the king's gaze, and the gaze has gone to the அரம்பையர். The verse echoes 291, where the king became a guest of the gods. The reason she gives for the renunciation is widowhood, not release.

353.reading: After removing the ornaments of her thighs, her ankle bells, anklets and toe rings, looking like a creeper whose flowers have bloomed and dropped, she puts on a fine cloth dyed in ochre while the goddesses cry out, saying 'May the mighty king's son rise.'
353.event: Vijayai puts on the ochre cloth of an ascetic, praying for her son's rise.
353.nuance: The vow that ends the stripping (349 to 353) is a wish for her son, உரவோன் சிறுவன் உயர்க: she takes the ascetic's cloth while keeping the one tie that the hermitage will not loosen (355, 359).

354.reading: When the good women held out milk-nectar in a gold vessel, the fish-eyed one would not even look at it; her forearm a kanthal-flower ladle, she cooked plain greens and became a deity dwelling in the forest.
354.event: Vijayai refuses the milk offered her and lives on greens she cooks herself.
354.nuance: வால் அடகு, plain leaf greens, is the widow's diet of the old poems, here taken up as tapas. வனத்து உறை தெய்வம் ஆனாள் makes the abstinence a kind of divinity.

355.reading: Where wild rice from the pond, gathered until her soft fingers grew thin, and the stamens of ripe water lilies dry in the courtyard, squirrels cry and scatter, and as the forest cow suckles its calf that clings to it, like a heap of moonbeams, she thinks of her son.
355.event: Seeing a forest cow suckling its calf, Vijayai remembers her son.
355.nuance: குள நெல் and ஆம்பல் அல்லி are the widow's foods of the old poems; the hermitage diet and the widow's merge. The scene of a beast nursing its young is what breaks the austerity's calm.

356.reading: Telling the ascetics, 'This lady, as though femininity, modesty, beauty, grace and innocence had gathered and taken form, is a charge entrusted to all of you who have received her', and keeping secret her land and her high lineage, the deity rose and went.
356.event: The deity entrusts Vijayai to the ascetic women, conceals her identity, and leaves.
356.nuance: அடைக்கலம் here is a person given into others' protection, not refuge at a god's feet; the giver of the charge is itself a deity. The concealment of land and lineage (நாடும் ... குலனும் ... கரந்து) keeps the queen hidden from the usurper.

357.reading: Because the companion, having weighed what was best, was eager to go there, the slender-waisted queen sent the hunchback away, telling her to learn how the beloved son of the white-umbrellaed king fared and come back by this road.
357.event: Vijayai sends the hunchback to learn news of her son and return.
357.nuance: Read with 356, the deity has already resolved to leave; the queen's errand only gives it the occasion. Who is the subject of உறுதி சூழ்ந்து அவண் ஓடலின் in line 1 is not fixed by the verse.

358.reading: Saying to herself, 'By my own nature I have deceived the one who is dear to me as my heart', the creeper-like companion went off with her many ornaments jingling and reached her own place in the walled city.
358.event: The deity, having left Vijayai under a pretext, returns to its own abode in the city.
358.nuance: The deity calls its kindly disguise a deceit (வஞ்சித்தேன்): it will not return with the news, and the queen's wait in 359 is the cost of the pretext.

359.reading: Vijayai herself, failing in spirit, stands watching the road by which the companion would return, and many days pass in longing in that honey-sweet grove of the hermitage.
359.event: Vijayai waits for days in the hermitage watching the road for news.
359.nuance: ஆனியம், taken here as 'days', is rare; the sense of a long wait is clear from the context.

360.reading: While the peacock-like woman with the honey-dripping garland and sword-bright eyes lives on there, the narrator turns to tell the learned all that happened on the other side.
360.nuance: The poet's own turn of the story (பகர்கு உற்றேன்), like 298 and 332, marking the shift from the mother to the son.

361.reading: The young merchant with the spear Death itself fears and his wife of steadfast chastity, together with the worthy elders they honoured and brought, gathered and named the renowned child Civakan of fierce strength.
361.event: Kantukkatan, his wife and the elders name the child Civakan.
361.nuance: The name answers the unseen voice that said சீவ when Kantukkatan sneezed over the child in 323. Whether the புண்ணியர் are invited elders or the couple themselves depends on how போற்றித் தந்த is construed.

362.reading: As the woman like lightning born of a cloud gives him the sweet nectar of her breasts, the child, like the great moon born of the sky, grows like an arrow shot by the meritorious one who yields delight.
362.event: Civakan grows up nursed by his foster mother.
362.nuance: The verse is built on ஈன்ற four times (born of the cloud, the breast, delight, the sky): the child is fed by a mother who did not bear him. Line 3's புண்ணியன் is not identified in the verse.

links.note: In 319 Vijayai cries that she has done no good deeds (நல் வினை செய்து இலாதேன்); 343 has the dawn drive off her night like evil deeds' suffering fleeing when old good deeds come forward.
links.teaches: The narrator quietly contradicts the mother's self-blame: the karma she said she lacked is the image he chooses for her deliverance, so her despair is shown to be mistaken about her own merit.

links.note: Naladiyar 51 uses lamp and darkness to state that sin cannot stand before austerity and returns when good deeds are spent; 343 makes the departure of darkness at sunrise a figure for evil deeds' suffering leaving when old merit comes forward, on the road to a hermitage.
links.teaches: The quatrain's doctrine becomes the epic's narrative weather: the dawn that ends Vijayai's flight is the merit-and-darkness image itself, placed just before she enters the very austerity the quatrain says sin cannot face.

gains.a: the dawn simile gains a doctrinal warrant, so the reader takes it as a forecast that her turn to tapas will hold off misfortune
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract lamp gains a dated moment in a life, a widow at sunrise on the way to the ascetics, where its rule is seen applied

links.note: Kural 378 says drily that the destitute would renounce if only fate let what they must suffer pass them by; 347 has a queen stripped of everything reach the ascetics' grove because a former-birth deed made her suffer.
links.teaches: The epic takes up the case the couplet treats as hypothetical: the destitute queen does renounce, and the following verses show the couplet's point surviving the renunciation, since her fated grief for her son goes on inside the hermitage.

gains.a: the verse gains a test of whether entering tapas ends the suffering the narrator ascribes to ஊழ்வினை, which the Kural answers in the negative
gains.b: the couplet's ironic 'if' gains a concrete instance in which renunciation is chosen from loss, not from strength

links.note: Kannaki, her husband killed by the king's error, asks whether she must waste away in grief like the women who keep hard observances when their husbands go to the pyre; Vijayai, her husband killed by a usurper, is led by the ascetic women into exactly such observances.
links.teaches: Two wronged wives face the same choice and the epics give opposite answers: Kannaki refuses the widow's penance and turns her grief on the city, while Vijayai accepts it and keeps her grief for a son still living, which shows the son as the difference.

links.note: In Purananuru 253 a wife whose husband fell asks how she can go among her kin raising an empty hand without bangles; in 351 Vijayai breaks her own bangles in a hermitage among ascetic women.
links.teaches: The widow's bare hand, which the Sangam wife dreads as a sign shown before her kin, becomes in the Jain epic an act the widow performs herself as part of an ascetic initiation among strangers.

gains.a: the breaking of bangles is shown to be the old widow's sign, so the initiation reads as widowhood as much as renunciation
gains.b: the Sangam poem's shame of the empty hand gains a later setting where the same sign is turned into a chosen discipline

links.note: Kural 341 holds that from whatever one has let go one suffers no pain; Vijayai lets go her ornaments one by one (349 to 353) but ends with a vow for her son, whom she does not let go and for whom she grieves in 355 and 359.
links.teaches: The piecemeal renunciation the couplet describes is acted out jewel by jewel, and the pain the couplet promises to remove returns exactly at the one tie the queen keeps, which shows the couplet's claim from its other side.

gains.a: the stripping scene gains a rule by which to measure it, so the son's survival in her vow reads as the unrenounced attachment
gains.b: the couplet's 'whatever, whatever' gains an ordered sequence of things given up and one thing held, with the pain located where letting go stops

links.note: Perunkoppendu refuses the widow's life of plain food, gravel bed and no ghee and chooses the pyre; Vijayai refuses the milk offered her and takes up a widow's diet of greens in the forest.
links.teaches: The diet the Sangam queen calls the lot of wretched widows and rejects for death is accepted by the epic's queen and renamed divinity (வனத்து உறை தெய்வம்), which shows how the Jain frame revalues the widow's abstinence the heroic poem despised.

gains.a: the verse's greens and refused milk are recognised as the widow's regimen, not only an ascetic's
gains.b: Perunkoppendu's scorn gains its counterpart, a queen who lives on and makes the same regimen a way of holiness

links.note: In Purananuru 248 the white water lily that was a girl's garment becomes the alli a widow eats; in 355 the stamens of ripe water lilies and wild rice dry in the hermitage courtyard as Vijayai's food.
links.teaches: The water lily carries the widow's fall from adornment to bare food in both poems, but in the epic the lily-food sits beside a nursing calf that sends her thoughts to her son, so the widow's diet is joined to a mother's longing the Sangam widow does not have.

gains.a: the passing detail of drying lily stamens is identified as the widow's food, so the hermitage scene is read as widowhood
gains.b: the Sangam widow's lily gains a later life in which the same food marks a mother waiting for her son

links.note: When Kantukkatan sneezed over the child in 323, a voice hidden in the branches said சீவ, 'live'; in 361 the child is named Civakan.
links.teaches: The hero's name is the fulfilment of an omen at his finding, so the name itself carries the blessing 'live' given over a child left in a burning ground.

links.note: In 355 the mother in the hermitage sees a forest cow suckling its calf and thinks of her son; in 362 the son drinks the milk of a foster mother and grows.
links.teaches: The nursing that Vijayai can only watch in a beast is happening to her own son at another woman's breast, so the two halves of the story are tied by the milk she cannot give.

links.note: In 314 a deity took the form of the hunchback Chanbakamalai, the maid who never left Vijayai's side; in 358 the deity leaves under the errand she gave it, calling its own guise a deceit.
links.teaches: The disguise that gave the queen comfort in her worst hour is the same means by which she is left alone, and the deity's own word for it, வஞ்சித்தேன், admits the cost of a kindness worked by pretence.

source_issues: Verses 340 and 348 to 356 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 340 line 1 (திருவில் கை போய் மெய் காப்ப) is obscure as printed.
Verse 349 lines 1 and 3 both open with திருந்து; the repetition may be original or a copying slip.
Verse 359 line 3 ஆனியம் is a rare word; verse 362 line 3 (போகம் ஈன்ற புண்ணியன் எய்த கணையே போல்) does not identify its புண்ணியன்.
